activity.title: Law and the Movement

readings.attribution: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, 347 U.S. 483 (1954), opinion of the Court by Chief Justice Earl Warren, May 17, 1954. Public domain (U.S. government work).
readings.body:
On segregating Black children in public schools: "To separate them from others of similar age and qualifications solely because of their race generates a feeling of inferiority as to their status in the community that may affect their hearts and minds in a way unlikely ever to be undone."

"We conclude that in the field of public education the doctrine of 'separate but equal' has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal."

About the case: NAACP lawyers led by Thurgood Marshall argued Brown and four related cases on behalf of Black families in Kansas, South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware and the District of Columbia. The decision was unanimous. A second ruling in 1955 ordered desegregation "with all deliberate speed," and many Southern officials responded with years of resistance.
readings.title: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka (1954), Chief Justice Warren for the Court, excerpts

readings.attribution: Civil Rights Act of 1964, Public Law 88-352, Title II, Section 201(a), signed July 2, 1964. Public domain (U.S. government work).
readings.body:
"All persons shall be entitled to the full and equal enjoyment of the goods, services, facilities, privileges, advantages, and accommodations of any place of public accommodation, as defined in this section, without discrimination or segregation on the ground of race, color, religion, or national origin."

About the source: Places of public accommodation included hotels, restaurants, theaters and gas stations. Other parts of the act barred discrimination in employment on the basis of race, color, religion, sex or national origin, and allowed the federal government to cut off funds to segregated programs. The act passed after the sit-in movement of 1960, the Freedom Rides of 1961, the Birmingham campaign and the March on Washington of 1963, and a Senate filibuster of more than fifty days.
readings.title: Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title II, Section 201(a)

readings.attribution: Lyndon B. Johnson, address to a joint session of Congress, March 15, 1965. Public domain (U.S. government work).
readings.body:
"At times history and fate meet at a single time in a single place to shape a turning point in man's unending search for freedom. So it was at Lexington and Concord. So it was a century ago at Appomattox. So it was last week in Selma, Alabama."

"There is no Negro problem. There is no Southern problem. There is no Northern problem. There is only an American problem."

"And we shall overcome."

Context: On March 7, 1965, state troopers and a sheriff's posse attacked peaceful voting rights marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama; television carried the pictures nationwide. Johnson spoke eight days later. "We shall overcome" was the anthem of the civil rights movement. Congress passed the Voting Rights Act in August 1965. The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) already said that the right to vote "shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude," but Southern states had used poll taxes, literacy tests and violence to keep most Black citizens from voting.
readings.title: Lyndon B. Johnson, Special Message to Congress: The American Promise (1965), excerpts
